whisper.label: Whisper Large-V3
whisper.text:
Hi, I'm Shohei Katayama. This is my piece, Ancient Voices, Glaciers. This is a landscape painting I
did out of strontium aluminate. The pigment actually has a half-life of 20 years, which
coincides with a timeline when the actual glaciers in the northern hemisphere is expected
to rapidly decay. So this painting eventually will be just like purely black. I participated
in an expedition through the Arctic Circle Residency. Part of the reason why I wanted
to go up there was to test for Fukushima radioisotopes in the form of cesium-134 and 137. The expedition
included scientists, educators, and artists.
I encountered a marine biologist who was talking about diatoms. Diatoms are integral
to the carbon cycle, or the carbon fixation process. These diatoms rely on calving glaciers
for nutrient. Without the glaciers, these nutrients will be provided to these larger
ecosystems so it can inevitably create an ecological collapse. So for me, this is more
like a time marker.
So I want to kind of tie in my personal narrative
of the radiation, my personal heritage with climate change, and therefore I decided to
use this material that I thought was pretty appropriate for the larger ecological context.
The audio that I use is from a GoPro that I put into the Arctic Ocean to catch different
sounds of deep ocean currents that are created through surge glaciers. The sea sponges is
more of a metaphor.
I'm going to show you a picture of a smaller subspecies that kind of rely onto these diatoms
because diatoms decay, they become into marine snow. Without sponges or these subspecies
that larger organisms rely onto, they are pretty much the foundation of the food pyramid,
right? So I wanted to kind of address the relationship between a macro environment with
micro systems like organisms.
So the blue that I'm using in this phosphorescent pigment is a blue that I'm using in the ocean.
So I'm going to use this blue to kind of show you the relationship between a macro environment
with micro systems like organisms.
So the blue that I'm using in this phosphorescent pigment is a blue that I'm using in the ocean.
It has like the same light frequency as real biological organisms, bioluminescence. It
is a phosphorescent pigment.
The material history has a strong correlation with radiation, especially in the U.S. It
kind of goes back with the radium girls. There is a cultural trope that radiation glows,
but in reality, of course, it doesn't glow. But there is this strong correlation between
it and the pop culture.
So for me, I like to play with light as an element.
Using strontium and luminate to talk about radiation as a larger theme.
